set.overview: Olancha Peak is the southernmost 12,000-footer of the Sierra crest, reached by a very long class 2 day from the desert side. The route climbs a steep canyon trail to Olancha Pass, runs north on the Pacific Crest Trail along the west side of the crest, then leaves the trail for roughly a mile of sand, trees and talus to a boulder-strewn summit. Distance and altitude, not difficulty, are the crux.
set.approach: Drive Sage Flat Road from US 395 near the town of Olancha: about three miles of pavement, then about three of rough gravel and dirt to the Sage Flat trailhead, which has parking and a stock camp. Walk the canyon trail steeply up to Olancha Pass, cross the meadow and wranglers' camp beyond it, and take the junction onto the Pacific Crest Trail heading north. Contour past high meadows and a small stream near 9,700 feet, then leave the trail at about 10,500 feet where the peak shows through the trees and climb the slope off-trail to the summit.
set.descent_text: Retrace the route: down the sandy, rocky slope to the Pacific Crest Trail, south to Olancha Pass, then down the canyon to the trailhead. Use the maintained switchback trail below the pass rather than the steep trampled cattle driveway beside it, which is hard-packed and slippery to descend.
hazards: Water is unreliable: the stream on the east side can be dry and the trickles on the crest dry up by afternoon, so carry plenty
The canyon trail below Olancha Pass is steep and chewed up by cattle, with braided paths that are easy to lose
Soft sand, loose pine debris and large boulders on the off-trail summit slope; drifting south brings class 3 moves
Strong wind and a big temperature swing between trailhead and summit
The last six miles of access road are rough gravel and hard on low cars

evidence.fact: 21.6 mi round trip, so about 10.8 mi one way
about 21 mi round trip, so about 10.5 mi one way

review.notes: A third trip report gives 19.1 mi and 7,800 ft (the 7,800 looks high); left out of the ledger. Gain and distance are round trip halved/as logged by two trip reports. Season skipped: reports span May-Aug but none states a window.

set.overview: Cartago Peak rises from the desert near the town of Cartago on the east side of the southern Sierra, and the standard climb is a steep, sandy slog of more than 6,000 feet in about five miles. The way is mostly class 2, up an old track, past two rock bands and onto a ridge. The true summit is the southernmost pinnacle at the southeast end of the summit plateau, finished with a few class 3 blocks.
set.approach: Turn off US 395 near the north end of Cartago onto an unsigned dirt road, cross the aqueduct and follow the aqueduct road south to a steep spur that ends at a wilderness boundary post near 4,000 feet. Parking at the post is tight; leaving the car on the aqueduct road adds about a quarter mile and 200 feet. Climb the wide old track and sandy slope to a first rock band, pass the second band, then reach the ridge near the saddle west of the 9,921-foot bump and continue to the plateau and the southeast pinnacle.
set.descent_text: A faster, gentler way down avoids the rock bands: from the large meadow east of the 9,921-foot bump, drop into the unnamed canyon that runs east to the aqueduct. It has little brush and easy sandy footing for plunge-stepping, and returns you to the car area in a few hours. Otherwise retrace the ascent and take care at the cliff bands.
hazards: Sandy slopes with poor footing and slipping for 2,000 feet or more
Two cliff bands low on the route with dense brush on the south side
Heat and swarming gnats on the lower desert face in spring
Snowbanks near 9,200 feet into late spring
Finding the true summit on the plateau, where several pinnacles look alike

evidence.fact: about 6,500 ft gain, about 4 mi one way
roughly 6,200 ft gain, about 10 mi round trip

review.notes: Distance skipped: 4 mi one way (1998) and about 5 mi one way (2006) differ by more than 10%. Assumed the standard route is the east-side Cartago Canal route; a PCT approach from Horseshoe Meadow also exists and was not used. Season skipped (reports are May and October, no window stated).

set.approach: Start from the Horseshoe Meadow trailhead above Lone Pine, where there are pit toilets, and walk the trail past a corral and through the meadows to Mulkey Pass, about 1.8 miles and 550 feet up. Drop roughly 700 feet toward the Diaz Creek drainage, cross the creek, and take the turnoff onto a cattle trail and then a use trail that follows the drainage between Muah Mountain and Peak 10,472. Follow cattle trails to the saddle between those two peaks.
set.descent_text: Retrace the route. From the summit a direct line down the sandy slopes toward Diaz Creek is quick, then climb back out of the drainage to Mulkey Pass and follow the trail down to the Horseshoe Meadow parking area. Expect to regain the 700 feet lost on the way in.
hazards: The 700-foot drop to Diaz Creek has to be climbed again at the end of the day
The summit is a narrow north-south fin of rocks with a false summit that is skirted to the south
Navigation relies on cattle and use trails and cross-country travel in foxtail pine forest
Cattle graze around the creek and can be startled

evidence.fact: about 12.1 mi round trip, halved to 6.05 mi one way

review.notes: One trip report only for gain and distance (the row's own description gives the same figures). A SummitPost snippet claiming 5,800 ft was not opened (blocked) and looks like a different approach. Season skipped.

set.overview: Cirque Peak is a broad 12,900-foot summit on the Sierra crest above Cottonwood Lakes, climbed more as a long hike than a scramble. From New Army Pass the north ridge is followed south over trail-less sand and rock past a series of false summits to the true top, a rise of about 600 feet in roughly two miles. A few short third-class bits are possible if the crest is hugged; keeping west of it is easier.
set.approach: Drive Horseshoe Meadow Road about 20 miles above Lone Pine to the Cottonwood Lakes trailhead. Hike the Cottonwood Lakes trail about 7.5 miles to New Army Pass at around 12,300 feet, the steepest part being the switchbacks just below the pass. From the pass go west across trail-less rock and sand, then follow the ridge as it turns south, staying just west of the crest, and pass under the false summits to the highest point.
set.descent_text: Return by the same ridge to New Army Pass and down the Cottonwood Lakes trail. A shorter alternative is to drop the south slope, which is much easier going down than up, to Cirque Lake, circle its north side and pick up the faint Old Cottonwood Creek trail back toward the trailhead.
hazards: Several false summits and trail-less terrain make the route-finding on the ridge easy to get wrong
Loose gravel and a slow boulder field if the Cirque Lake side is used
The Old Cottonwood Creek trail fades out near Cirque Lake and is hard to find
A long, strenuous day at 12,000 feet with exposure to wind and afternoon weather

evidence.fact: about 19 mi out and back, roughly 2,900 ft gain via New Army Pass
19 mi round trip, halved to 9.5 mi one way; pass is 7.5 mi from the trailhead plus about 2 mi to the summit

review.notes: Second source for gain/distance not found (Peakery log page was empty; a search summary of 16.8 mi / 3,341 ft is not evidence). Third-class mention comes from the row's own grade, not an opened page. Season skipped.

set.overview: Mount Pickering is a 13,400-foot peak above Miter Basin in Sequoia National Park, reached from Sky Blue Lake by a steep class 2 climb. The route follows a depression between Pickering and Mount Newcomb to a saddle left of the summit, then boulders to the top. The summit climb is short, but the miles in from the trailhead make it a multi-day or very long trip.
set.approach: From the Cottonwood Lakes trailhead on Horseshoe Meadow Road, follow the New Army Pass trail to Lower Soldier Lake on Rock Creek, then continue up Miter Basin to Sky Blue Lake at about 11,550 feet. Follow the creek to the back of the lake, cross to the depression between Pickering and Newcomb, climb about 1,500 feet of steep slope to the saddle left of the summit, and finish up about 500 feet of boulders.
set.descent_text: Go back down the way you came to Sky Blue Lake and Soldier Lake. A direct sand chute between Pickering and Newcomb is a quick way down. Avoid the southeast ridge toward Primrose Lake, which is harder than its class 2 rating suggests.
hazards: Loose gravel and lingering snow patches on the steep slope to the saddle
Large boulders near the top slow the final stretch
A tall waterfall near Sky Blue Lake means staying on the west side to avoid cliffs
The southeast ridge toward Primrose Lake has class 3 and some class 4 moves

review.notes: Gain/distance skipped: only one source (30 mi round trip, 3,500 ft), and that trip's gain looks too low for the stated route. Season skipped.

set.approach: Every approach is long and needs a Mount Whitney Zone permit. The shortest, about 12 miles, takes the Whitney Trail to Trail Crest, then drops cross-country down scree into the Crabtree basin. A longer version of about 17 miles and 5,000 feet of gain follows the John Muir Trail past Guitar Lake and leaves it at the Crabtree Ranger Station for a rougher trail into the Crabtree Lakes basin. The route starts up the left side of the central buttress on the north face, through dirty third-class ledges to an alcove.
hazards: Poor rock on the upper pitches, especially pitch 4, with loose knobs and flakes
Sparse gear and long runouts on pitch 5 and again higher
Dirty ledges on the opening scramble
Shifting scree on the cross-country approach and a dangerous gully near the Trail Crest talus

review.notes: Both sources are Mountain Project (one publisher). Descent skipped: the area page names a gully between Chamberlin and Crabtree Crags but not for this route. Season skipped: access is limited May-Oct in the zone but no window for the climb is stated. Gain/distance skipped.

set.overview: Mount Newcomb is a 13,400-foot peak above the Crabtree Lakes on the Sierra crest, and its southwest slope is the easy side: sandy slopes and stable class 2 rock lead to the summit plateau. The ridge approach from Crabtree Pass is harder and slower, with class 3 sections. Most climbers take the Perrin Creek side or the Whitney Portal route over Discovery Pass.
set.approach: From the Whitney Portal side, climb the Whitney Trail past Trail Camp and the switchbacks, scramble over boulders to Discovery Pass, drop about 1,000 feet into the Crabtree drainage and climb to Crabtree Pass; the ridge from there is slower than it looks and reaches class 3. From the Cottonwood Lakes side, cross Old Army Pass to Rock Creek, find the obscure start of Perrin Creek, camp at the first lake of the upper basin, and cross a sand traverse to stable class 2 rock leading up to the plateau.
set.descent_text: Come down the southwest slope, an easy class 2 descent at a modest angle, or use the second-class chute on the east side that reaches the southwest corner of the summit plateau. From there return to Perrin Creek or Crabtree Pass and your approach route.
hazards: The ridge between Crabtree Pass and the summit is class 3 and costs far more time than the map suggests
Loose sand chutes on the upper slopes
Boulder field in lower Perrin Creek and a hard-to-find start
Perrin Creek holds little water until just below the lake basin; carry water

review.notes: Gain/distance skipped: pages opened give no figure for a single approach (Peakery loop figure of 25.5 mi is a different loop). Season skipped.

set.approach: The line is on the long northeast face of Mount Hitchcock in Sequoia National Park. The first-ascent party hiked over the Whitney-Russell col and camped at a small tarn roughly 500 feet below Arctic Lake before walking to the base. From Whitney Portal the longer route of about 17 miles via the John Muir Trail past Guitar Lake and the Crabtree Ranger Station is the usual way to reach the Hitchcock buttresses, and a Mount Whitney Zone permit is needed.
hazards: The moderate slab linking the lower dihedrals to the upper corner is very run-out
Snow can cover the scramble to the base early in the season
A 5.9 offwidth in the upper corner and 5.11 overhangs make the route hard to retreat from
Remote location with a long approach and no easy escape

review.notes: Descent skipped (AAC report says only that the party descended the route). Gain/distance/season skipped. The 17 mile Whitney Portal figure comes from the Chamberlin area page and is a general approach to the Crabtree basin, not measured to this base.
